clue.text: The principal, Copperfield's schoolmaster, is self-willed

parts.note: the head is the principal of a school
Doctor Strong keeps the school David attends in Dickens's David Copperfield

explanation.surface: A headmaster from a Dickens novel is described as wilful.
explanation.walkthrough: The schoolmaster in David Copperfield is Dr Strong; 'The principal' gives HEAD, so the clue reads as a school's head being obstinate.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone obstinate and determined to have their own way is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Hear that man sing it

indicators.note: the instruction to listen means the word for that man is taken as it is spoken

parts.note: him is the pronoun for that man

explanation.surface: An instruction to listen to a man singing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear' tells you to take HIM by its sound; a sacred song you sing is spelt HYMN.
explanation.definitionFit: A church song is the thing a congregation is asked to sing.

clue.text: Bristol port

parts.note: the docks of the English city of Bristol lie at the mouth of its river

explanation.surface: A plain description of a harbour in the West of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Bristol is a city in south-west England; its docks stand where the River Avon meets the Severn estuary.
explanation.definitionFit: The district and docks at the river mouth serve as the city's seaport.

clue.text: James is neat when not forthcoming

annotationWithheld.why: James is neat when not forthcoming (5): 'neat when not forthcoming' gives a bullock (STEER), but no reading found of what 'James is' contributes
annotationWithheld.clue: James is neat when not forthcoming

clue.text: Even in the pram 'e's escorted royally

definitions.text: Even in the pram 'e's escorted royally

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words 'pram 'e's escorted'

explanation.surface: A Cockney nanny remarks that even in his pram the little one travelled like royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: The name of the pharaoh runs across 'pRAM 'E'S ESscorted'; the whole clue pictures a royal baby attended even in a pram.
explanation.definitionFit: A pharaoh of ancient Egypt would be escorted royally from the cradle.

clue.text: One who grudges to pull: a trap up

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' means the pieces are read from the bottom upward

parts.note: to drag is to pull
a gin is a snare or trap

explanation.surface: Someone resents being made to haul a trap uphill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns DRAG + GIN, which is DRAGGIN, into the miser's word.
explanation.definitionFit: A miser who begrudges spending or giving is a stingy person.

clue.text: Meat strike

definitions.meaning: a cut of pork or lamb with a rib
to hit with a sharp downward blow

explanation.definitionFit: A cutlet of lamb or pork and a short cutting blow share the same word.

clue.text: Accommodation for stay-makers

parts.note: stay-makers suggests corsetry workers, but read as people making a stay it means guests

explanation.surface: Lodgings for workers who make corset stays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stay-makers' looks like corset makers (stays are corset stiffeners); really it is people who make a stay somewhere as guests.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn offers rooms to travellers who stop for a night or more.

clue.text: Greengrocer's cheapest source of vitamin C? It grows wild

definitions.text: Greengrocer's cheapest source of vitamin C?
definitions.meaning: a salad cress costing a single coin of the lowest value
a wild plant of the cabbage family found in fields

explanation.definitionFit: The weed's name reads as a cress costing one penny, the cheapest salad green, and it is a wild field plant.

clue.text: Spoiled with a lamp in bed

indicators.note: the lamp's word is placed inside the word for bed

parts.note: taken as written
a lamp is a light

explanation.surface: Someone's night was ruined by a lamp left on in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is only a link; 'in' signals the container, and 'Spoiled' at the front is the definition, not a description of the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Crops ruined by disease, or hopes ruined by misfortune, are described this way.

clue.text: Thomas finds love in Sir Thomas

indicators.note: the zero is placed inside the statesman's surname

parts.note: Sir Thomas More, the Tudor statesman and author of Utopia
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: One Thomas discovers affection in another Thomas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finds ... in' puts O (love, nil in tennis) inside MORE; the result is the surname of Thomas Moore, the Irish poet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish poet of Irish Melodies bore this forename, so the given name points to his surname.

clue.text: All for cricket, in a Pickwickian sense

definitions.text: All for cricket, in a Pickwickian sense

parts.words: All for cricket, in a Pickwickian sense
parts.note: in Pickwick Papers the Dingley Dell side plays a cricket match against the team from a town prefixed All-

explanation.surface: Someone is all in favour of cricket, in the spirit of Mr Pickwick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All for cricket' reads as keenness, but in The Pickwick Papers 'All' is the first half of a town's name, All-Muggleton, whose team plays Dingley Dell.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's fictional town completes the name of the cricket team that plays Dingley Dell.

clue.text: Why sob, Maria-the food was divine !

indicators.note: the startled exclamation suggests the letters that follow are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Someone asks Maria why she is crying, since the meal was heavenly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Why' signals the anagram: the letters of SOB and MARIA are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the gods ate this, so it was literally divine fare.

clue.text: Channel off pitch

definitions.meaning: a gutter or narrow ravine cut by water
a cricket fielding position on the off side near the batsman

explanation.definitionFit: A narrow water-worn ravine and an off-side cricket fielding position share one word.

clue.text: Ceres' hair-do ?

parts.note: Ceres is the Roman goddess of corn and harvest, so her braid would be woven from stalks

explanation.surface: A question about how a Roman goddess wears her hair.
explanation.walkthrough: Ceres is the Roman goddess of cereal crops, so a plait for her hair would be woven of corn stalks; the name is that of braided straw used for hats.
explanation.definitionFit: Braided stems of corn used in hat-making suit the goddess of grain as a braid.

clue.text: Successfully tells an affecting tale to extract 'money

definitions.text: Successfully tells an affecting tale to extract 'money

parts.words: Successfully tells an affecting tale to extract 'money
parts.note: to get a loan or gift out of someone by a moving story is to hit them up for cash

explanation.surface: A con artist spins a sob story and gets paid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affecting' points to the sense of moving someone; the same verb means wheedling money out of someone ('he touched me for a fiver').
explanation.definitionFit: Getting money from someone by appeal is the slang sense of this verb, which also means moving emotionally.

clue.text: He hadn't 'so much we hear, and was' unconcerned

indicators.note: the phrase means what follows is judged by its sound

parts.note: he had less, shortened to he'd less

explanation.surface: A man who had less than others did not mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' says 'he'd less' (he hadn't so much) sounds like the word for careless.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking no notice of warnings or danger means being careless and unbothered.

clue.text: Agricultural worker, down in the drink

definitions.meaning: a labourer who digs and clears field drains
one who ditches, bringing an aircraft down in the sea

explanation.definitionFit: A farm labourer who digs drains, and a pilot who brings a plane down on water, are both described by this word.

clue.text: Salute the flag in a wintry storm?

parts.note: to hail is to greet or salute
a flag is a paving stone, a flagstone

explanation.surface: Someone salutes the flag during a winter blizzard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the flag' looks like a banner, but a flag is also a flat paving stone.
explanation.definitionFit: A pellet of ice that falls in a winter storm.

clue.text: Lockwood's bunch ?

parts.note: split as lock and wood: a bunch of things for locks from a kind of timber

explanation.surface: A question about a group belonging to someone called Lockwood.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'Lockwood' into lock and wood: a bunch of keys (for a lock) from a tree (wood); the winged seeds of the ash tree hang in bunches called keys.
explanation.definitionFit: The ash tree's winged seeds hang in clusters called keys.

clue.text: Tasteful needlework

parts.note: embroidery that is also a taster

explanation.surface: Elegant embroidery.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is both one who tastes a sample and a piece of embroidery showing stitches, so 'Tasteful' points to the tasting sense.
explanation.definitionFit: An embroidered panel displaying stitches and letters shares its name with one who tries a little of something.

clue.text: T boys ? Sound idea

parts.note: boys at the golf tee, a sound like tea

explanation.surface: A suggestion that boys called T would be a good idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'T' sounds like tee (golf) and tea: boys who carry clubs to the tee, and boxes that hold tea, share this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Golf bag-carriers and tea containers share one name, matched by tee and tea.

clue.text: Thomas came further south of the Border than his name suggests

definitions.text: Thomas came further south of the Border than his name suggests

parts.words: Thomas came further south of the Border than his name suggests
parts.note: the Scottish writer's surname sounds like the English border city Carlisle, yet he settled in London

explanation.surface: A man named Thomas moved further into England than his surname implies.
explanation.walkthrough: The Border is the Scotland-England border; the Scottish essayist's surname sounds like Carlisle, the city just south of it, but he went on to live in Chelsea, London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian essayist Thomas, Sage of Chelsea, was born in Scotland.

clue.text: Flower-pattern plate

indicators.note: a pattern means the letters are set out in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A plate decorated with flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pattern' signals the anagram of PLATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Part of a bloom, one of its coloured leaves, stands for the flower.

clue.text: They wage war on caterpillars

parts.note: armoured vehicles that run on caterpillar tracks

explanation.surface: Gardeners waging war on pests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on caterpillars' reads as attacking pests but means riding on caterpillar tracks, the treads of armoured fighting vehicles.
explanation.definitionFit: Armoured fighting vehicles move on caterpillar tracks and fight battles.

clue.text: One who preaches ethics by word of mouth in a fog

indicators.note: the spoken word is placed inside the fog

parts.note: mist is a light fog
oral means spoken

explanation.surface: A preacher gives spoken sermons in a haze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'word of mouth' means spoken, not rumour; 'in' signals the container, with 'by' a link before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who lectures others on right and wrong is a preacher of morals.

clue.text: Wild zeal to come by a copper didn't work

indicators.note: wild means the letters are scattered out of order

parts.note: d stood for the old British penny, a copper coin

explanation.surface: Wild enthusiasm arrives with a policeman, so nobody worked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' makes LAZE from ZEAL; a copper is D, the old British penny (from Latin denarius), not a policeman.
explanation.definitionFit: To idle away time is to do no work.

clue.text: One double bend after another of the river

indicators.note: the pair of pieces is repeated, one copy following the other

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
the letter S has the shape of a double bend

explanation.surface: Someone counts the bends of a river one after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after another' repeats I + S; the result is the name of the Thames at Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: At Oxford the Thames is known by this name.

clue.text: Shy of her ? Relatively

parts.note: a coconut shy at a fair features a figure named after a female relative

explanation.surface: Someone is bashful about a woman who is a relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shy' means a throw at a fair, not bashful: the fairground figure that people throw things at is named for a parent's sister, hence 'Relatively'.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairground target figure is a dummy pelted with balls, and her name begins with a relation.

clue.text: Climbs steeply out of Lens?

parts.note: Lens is a French town, but here a camera lens of variable focal length

explanation.surface: An aircraft climbs sharply away from the French town of Lens.
explanation.walkthrough: Lens looks like the French town; really a variable-focus camera lens shares this word for steep climbing.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft that climbs steeply does this, and the variable camera lens is named with the same word.

clue.text: Streamlined cricket

parts.note: a shortened, international form of the game

explanation.surface: A sleek version of the game of cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: An international cricket match between countries is called this; 'Streamlined' suggests a trial run, as in a wind tunnel.
explanation.definitionFit: International cricket matches are named after a trial, and a trial is an examination.

clue.text: Such as have opals?

parts.note: split opals as O pals, nought pals, people with no companions

explanation.surface: A question about people who own precious opals.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'opals' as O (nought) pals: those with zero pals.
explanation.definitionFit: People without companions are lonely ones.
